media:group.media:title: Mayo Clinic Minute: Hypertension and heart disease in the Black community
media:group.media:description:
Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in the U.S. African Americans are significantly affected by heart disease, resulting in higher mortality rates compared to white Americans.
One of the reasons for the disparity is the high hypertension rates in the Black community. Hypertension, also known as high blood pressure, can increase your risk of developing heart disease.

entry.title: A Nonsurgical Weight-Loss Option: Endoscopic Sleeve Gastroplasty (ESG) at Mayo Clinic

media:group.media:title: A Nonsurgical Weight-Loss Option: Endoscopic Sleeve Gastroplasty (ESG) at Mayo Clinic
media:group.media:description:
Daniel B. Maselli, M.D., gastroenterologist at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, explains how this same-day procedure is used to reshape and reduce stomach size without incisions or removing or rerouting the digestive tract. Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG) offers patients an effective, less-invasive alternative to bariatric surgery within Mayo Clinic's comprehensive obesity-care model.
Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG) is a minimally invasive, non-surgical weight-loss procedure that reduces the size of the stomach without external incisions or removing or rerouting any part of the digestive tract.
During ESG, a flexible endoscope is passed through the mouth into the stomach. Using an endoscopic suturing device, a physician places a series of stitches that shorten and narrow the stomach from the inside, reducing its size by approximately 70% to 80%. The procedure creates a sleeve-like shape that helps patients feel satisfied with smaller portions and stay satisfied longer after eating.
When combined with nutritional support, ESG can help patients lose approximately 18% to 20% of their body weight over the course of a year. Benefits may extend beyond weight loss, with improvements in quality of life and weight-related conditions such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, fatty liver disease, sleep apnea and joint pain.
ESG is performed as a same-day procedure and typically involves a shorter recovery than bariatric surgery. Most patients are ready to return to work within about three to four days.
Learn how Mayo Clinic’s multidisciplinary team approaches ESG and obesity treatment with individualized care before, during and after the procedure.

entry.title: Bone health: What to eat for stronger bones | Mayo Clinic On Nutrition Podcast

media:group.media:title: Bone health: What to eat for stronger bones | Mayo Clinic On Nutrition Podcast
media:group.media:description:
What should you eat for strong, healthy bones? Calcium matters, but maintaining bone health involves much more than simply drinking milk.
In this episode of On Nutrition, registered dietitian Tara Schmidt talks with registered dietitian Melissa Mitri, MS, RDN, about how nutrition and exercise can help support bone health throughout your life. They explain when bone loss begins, the difference between osteopenia and osteoporosis and why menopause can accelerate bone loss.
Learn which foods provide calcium, vitamin D, protein and other nutrients important for healthy bones, including options for people who don't consume dairy. They also discuss calcium and vitamin D supplements, the potential connection between prunes and bone health and emerging research on the gut-bone axis.
Plus, learn how strength training and weight-bearing exercise can support bone health, what people with osteopenia or osteoporosis should consider before exercising and what the research says about weighted vests and vibration plates.
In this episode, you'll learn: • When bone loss begins • Signs of declining bone health • The difference between osteopenia and osteoporosis • How menopause affects bone density • Which nutrients help support strong bones • The best food sources of calcium and vitamin D • When calcium or vitamin D supplements may be helpful • Why prunes may benefit bone health • How strength training and weight-bearing exercise help bones • What to know about weighted vests and vibration plates

media:group.media:title: Craniofacial Planning & Reconstruction, Neurosurgical Navigation
media:group.media:description:
How can artificial intelligence, 3D surface scanning, and advanced engineering improve brain surgery?
In this presentation, Dr. Kendall Lee, Professor of Neurosurgery and Biomedical Engineering at Mayo Clinic, shares innovations that are changing the field of stereotactic and functional neurosurgery. He discusses the development of the D1 and E1 surgical frames, advances in deep brain stimulation (DBS), AI-assisted surgical planning, and the use of 3D facial scanning as an alternative to traditional CT-based registration methods.
The talk explores how multidisciplinary collaboration among neurosurgeons, engineers, anatomists, and software developers is accelerating innovation for patients with Parkinson's disease, tremor, dystonia, obsessive-compulsive disorder, epilepsy, and other neurological conditions.
Topics include: Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) Parkinson's disease treatment AI-assisted surgical planning 3D facial scanning for surgical navigation Frameless stereotactic neurosurger Neuroengineering and precision surgery Medical device innovation The MAVEN neuromodulation platform The future of functional neurosurgery

entry.title: CAR-T cell therapy for large B-cell lymphoma: A patient’s story | John Renze

media:group.media:title: CAR-T cell therapy for large B-cell lymphoma: A patient’s story | John Renze
media:group.media:description:
11-18-26 Set private due to copyright claim. Spoke with Kevin Sullivan. He sent licenses, I am disputing and keeping requesters in the loop. (Tim)
Lymphoma survivor John Renze shares his experience with stage 4 large B-cell lymphoma and CAR-T cell therapy at Mayo Clinic.
After chemotherapy, radiation therapy and participation in clinical studies did not eliminate his cancer, John qualified in 2016 for a Mayo Clinic clinical trial evaluating chimeric antigen receptor-T cell therapy, also known as CAR-T cell therapy, for large B-cell lymphoma. After receiving his CAR-T cell infusion, his first scan showed no evidence of cancer.
In this patient Q&A, John talks about his lymphoma diagnosis, cancer treatment journey, CAR-T cell therapy experience and life after treatment. He also reflects on what it means to remain in remission and return to everyday life, including working, farming and spending time with his children and grandchildren.
Hear directly from a lymphoma patient and survivor about CAR-T cell therapy, living with and beyond cancer, and his experience receiving treatment at Mayo Clinic.

media:group.media:title: Obesity Pharmacotherapy with Dr. Kristina Thurber
media:group.media:description:
Obesity medications are changing the way we approach weight management, but with rapidly evolving treatment options come important questions about effectiveness, safety, and long-term use. In this podcast, we are joined by Mayo Clinic pharmacist, Dr. Kristina Thurber, to discuss the evolving landscape of obesity pharmacotherapy. We explore GLP-1 medications and other treatment options, realistic expectations for weight loss, managing side effects, and what happens when treatment is discontinued. Tune in for a practical discussion of what patients and clinicians should know about medical weight management.

entry.title: The New Era of Obesity Medications: What’s Changing in Cardiovascular Care

media:group.media:title: The New Era of Obesity Medications: What’s Changing in Cardiovascular Care
media:group.media:description:
Guest: Kyla Lara-Breitinger, M.D., M.S. Host: Stephen Kopecky, M.D.
GLP-1 receptor agonists are changing the way clinicians think about obesity—not simply as a weight issue, but as a cardiometabolic disease with important cardiovascular implications. Dr. Kyla Lara-Breitinger discusses how medications such as semaglutide and tirzepatide may benefit patients with obesity and related conditions, including cardiovascular disease, HFpEF, chronic kidney disease, and obstructive sleep apnea.
The conversation explores practical considerations for prescribing these medications, from patient selection and insurance coverage to hydration, protein intake, resistance training, and preserving muscle mass during weight loss. Drs. Lara-Breitinger and Kopecky also discuss maintenance strategies, the importance of pairing medication with sustainable lifestyle changes, and promising next-generation obesity therapies on the horizon.
Topics discussed:
• How are GLP-1 receptor agonists changing the cardiologist’s role in treating obesity and reducing cardiovascular risk? • Which patients may benefit from obesity medications, including those with cardiovascular disease, HFpEF, chronic kidney disease, or obstructive sleep apnea? • How can clinicians help patients manage side effects while maintaining adequate hydration, protein, fiber, and muscle mass during weight loss? • What role do resistance training and sustainable lifestyle changes play alongside GLP-1 medications? • Are obesity medications likely to require long-term maintenance, and what emerging therapies could shape the next era of treatment?
